title: ReAct Teaching Note
text: ReAct combines reasoning traces with actions in an interleaved loop. The agent reasons about what information or action is needed, invokes an external tool or environment action, observes the result, and continues reasoning. This design connects reasoning and acting instead of treating them as separate phases. ReAct trajectories can improve interpretability because actions and observations remain visible in the task path.

title: RAG Teaching Note
text: Retrieval-augmented generation separates parametric model knowledge from retrieved external evidence. A retriever selects passages from a corpus and a generator uses those passages to answer. Retrieval quality and answer grounding are separate concerns: finding a passage does not guarantee that the final answer cites or interprets it correctly. RAG is especially useful when knowledge should be updated without retraining the language model.

title: Reflexion Teaching Note
text: Reflexion gives a language agent verbal feedback about prior attempts and stores reflective text that can influence later behavior. The method focuses on learning from trial outcomes through language feedback rather than updating model weights. Reflection can improve future trajectories, but an engineering system still needs explicit limits so repeated self-critique does not become an unbounded loop.

title: Multi-Agent Teaching Note
text: A multi-agent system can separate specialist responsibilities, context, tools, and authority. A supervisor can delegate bounded review tasks to a critic and optional writer while retaining control of the user-facing workflow. Multiple agents are not automatically better: coordination adds latency, cost, routing errors, and new security boundaries, so the architecture should be evaluated against a simpler baseline.
